newsitem.title: GERMANY: German plant breeders back transgenic EU maize.
newsitem.headline: German plant breeders back transgenic EU maize.

text.p: The Federation of German Plant Breeders (BDP) supported the European Union (EU) reaching a decision in favour of gene-modified maize cultivation in the EU, managing director Ferdinand Schmitz said on Wednesday.
The EU is assessing an application for maize produced by Swiss chemical firm Ciba Geigy AG.
"This decision will be of enormous significance to some 20 companies working on maize within our 100-strong membership," Schmitz said during a maize promotion event.
"We have urged the EU to find a quick solution," he added.
Delays to the EU's approval process -- as some member states are worried too little is known about environmental impacts -- slowed seed marketing efforts for 1997 spring plantings, Schmitz added.
The Ciba corn has been made resistant to certain pesticides and the highly damaging European corn borer.
U.S. farmers, who have sown some 200,000 hectares to genetically-modified maize this year, also want EU access.

Other speakers at the press conference, which was organised by the producer-funded German maize committee DMK, also supported the use of biotechnology to make starch-rich maize crops resistant to pests and to raise yields.
"There is no alternative to an ecologically sound use of genetic modifications if maize growers want to keep up with population and incomes rises," said Hugo Steinhauser of Munich University.
Maize crops were broadly similar in numbers with wheat and rice -- 550 million tonnes will be produced in 1996 -- but its high yields meant it needed a smaller area, he said.
The world's arable area would decline by 40 percent by the year 2020 due to population growth.
Agronomist Rudolf Stoehr of grain trader Alfred Toepfer said eastern European countries such as Poland, Romania, Hungary, the Ukraine and Slovakia could produce more maize.

This could help offset the world market's dependency on the U.S., South Africa and Latin America, where water availability, weather patterns and competiton with other crops created volatile crop patterns.
